problem: Object-centric LLM/VLM navigation does not transfer to structured buildings (offices, hotels) organized by room numbers and signs. LLM-as-end-to-end-planner methods hallucinate, loop, and lack spatial grounding, while pure frontier exploration ignores semantic cues and is inefficient.
motivation: Humans use signs and room-numbering schemes to infer where a goal room lies before seeing it. Robots that only build geometric maps explore inefficiently in large buildings. Combining LLM pattern inference with classical exploration keeps completeness while gaining efficiency.
key_idea: Query an LLM periodically on the partially observed occupancy and semantic grids to predict the goal's direction, accumulate these predictions in a decaying confidence grid, and navigate to the highest-confidence region, falling back to frontier exploration with A*.
insight: The LLM supplies only a coarse directional hypothesis (right/left/up/down) that biases exploration. Frontier fallback and A* provide reliability and coverage, and confidence decay with reset of explored cells corrects wrong hypotheses. Baselines show the split of roles: LLM Only loops or collides (SPL 0.05 on large maps), Frontier Exploration always succeeds but is inefficient (SPL 0.65), and the hybrid reaches SPL 0.74. Failures appear when numbering is ambiguous (600A-C near 617) or labels are sparse. No formal component ablation is reported beyond these baselines.
method: Goal extraction: an LLM parses the command (e.g. 'Go to Room 621') into a goal identifier string.
Perception grids: SeenOccupancyGrid (-1 for unknown) and SeenSemanticGrid are updated from a local k×k window each step.

LLM prediction: given both seen grids and the agent position, the LLM outputs reasoning, inferred patterns (e.g. numbers increase to the right, odd/even sides) and a predicted goal region (right/left/up/down relative to the agent).
Confidence grid: a belief heatmap of zeros; cells in the predicted direction get +1, all values decay by α each step, and explored non-goal cells are reset to 0.

Planning: if the goal is seen, plan A* to it. Otherwise A* to the centroid of the highest-confidence region, and if the centroid equals the agent position, fall back to the nearest frontier; execute the first action.
Real-robot deployment: a pre-annotated grid map is anchored to Spot's odometry frame via a calibration cell, and SE(2) waypoints are sent through the Boston Dynamics API.

setting.backbone: unspecified LLM (frozen, prompted) + A* + frontier exploration
setting.observation: local k×k window of ground-truth occupancy and semantic (sign / room-number text) grid cells
setting.action_space: 4 discrete grid moves (up, down, left, right)
setting.simulator: custom 2D grid worlds (from floor plans and a Polycam scan); Spot real-world demo
setting.privileged: room numbers and signs are explicitly annotated in the semantic grid; full observability of the k×k window; a pre-annotated grid map for the real robot

results: The method achieves an SPL of 0.745 overall, versus 0.596 for Frontier Exploration, 0.236 for NavGPT and 0.160 for LLM-Only, with paths over 40% shorter than alternatives. Frontier Exploration keeps SR 1.00 everywhere, while the proposed method has a slightly lower SR (0.80-0.97) due to timeouts. On Large Offices it is slightly worse than frontier exploration (SPL 0.53 vs 0.56). A real Spot deployment reached room 621.
limitations: Signs and room numbers are ground-truth annotated on the grid and perception is a full k×k window, so there is no real sign or text recognition.
Performance degrades on noisy maps and with ambiguous numbering (e.g. 600A-C near 617), and near-uniform LLM predictions when labels are sparse slow convergence.
Evaluation is on a few 2D grid environments with only 10 episodes each, and the real-robot test is a single qualitative run on a pre-annotated map.
